title: Enuma Elish, Tablet VI: the creation of humankind and of Babylon
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.2, Poem of Creation (Enuma elish) (ed. A. C. Heinrich, rev. Z. J. Földi and E. Jiménez), SB VI) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: Enuma Elish (the Babylonian Poem of Creation), Tablet VI: 125 of 166 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (13 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
Ea creates humankind from the blood of the guilty god Qingu to bear the gods' labour. The gods build Babylon and the temple Esagil for Marduk, hold a banquet, and begin to proclaim his fifty names.

Enuma Elish ('When on high'), the Babylonian Poem of Creation, tells how Marduk, god of Babylon, defeated Tiamat, created the ordered world and became king of the gods. It was written on seven tablets and recited in Babylon during the New Year festival. The date of composition is debated (proposals range from the 18th to the 12th century BCE); the surviving copies date from the 9th to the 2nd century BCE and come from Ashur, Nineveh, Kish, Babylon, Sippar, Uruk and other sites. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/2/SB/VI) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed manuscript with the most signs preserved there. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives. Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the poem; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 125 of the 166 lines of the eBL edition (75%), from 13 tablets in the British Museum: K.3567 (Nineveh), BM.33572, K.12000.B (Nineveh), BM.33690, BM.54855, BM.38043, K.3449.A (Nineveh), K.9883 (Nineveh), K.13867 (Nineveh), BM.55380, K.5923 (Nineveh), K.13865 (Nineveh), BM.54311.

Lines not shown. 41 of the 166 lines of the eBL edition have no witness here with an open photograph: 8 (only on VAT.9676, VAT.11363, IM.121284, BM.92629, Ashm-1924.1828); 9-12 (only on VAT.9676, IM.121284, BM.92629, Ashm-1924.1828); 13-20 (only on VAT.9676, SU-1951.237, IM.121284, BM.92629, Ashm-1924.1828); 61-64 (only on VAT.9676, SU-1952.60, IM.121284, Ashm-1924.1828, unnumbered); 65-67 (only on VAT.9676, SU-1952.60, IM.121284, unnumbered); 71-73 (only on VAT.9676, SU-1952.60, IM.121284, unnumbered); 111-112 (only on VAT.9676, SU-1952.60, IM.121284, Ashm-1924.1828); 113 (only on SU-1952.60, IM.121284, Ashm-1924.1828, VAT.9676); 114-116 (only on VAT.9676, SU-1952.60, IM.121284, Ashm-1924.1828); 127-129 (only on VAT.9676, SU-1952.60, IM.121284, Ashm-1924.1828); 158-165 (only on VAT.9676, Ist-A.512, IM.121284, BM.92629, Ashm-1924.1828); 166 (only on VAT.9676, Ist-A.512, IM.121284, BM.92629). Lines that survive only on tablets whose photographs are not openly licensed (for example in the Iraq Museum, Berlin, Istanbul, Ankara, Philadelphia or private collections), or only on tablets whose eBL photograph does not show the lines, are omitted.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

translation.text:
21Let your first reply be the truth!
22Do you speak with me truthful words!
23“Who was it that started the war,
24“Suborned Tiamat and drew up for battle?
25“Let him be given over to me, the one who started the war,
26“I shall make him bear his punishment, you shall dwell in peace.”
27The Igigi, the great gods answered him,
28To Lugaldimmeankia, counselor of the gods, their lord,
29“It was Qingu who made war,
30“Suborned Tiamat and drew up for battle.”
31They bound and held him before Ea,
32They imposed the punishment on him and shed his blood.
33From his blood they (Marduk and Ea) made humankind,
34He imposed the toil of the gods and the gods (from it).
35After Ea the wise had made humankind,
36And had imposed the toil of the gods on them —
37That deed is beyond comprehension,
38By the artifices of Marduk did Nudimmud create —
39Marduk the king divided the gods,
40All the Anunna-gods, all of them, into upper and lower,
41He assigned to Anu for duty at his command.
42Three hundred he posted in heaven for duty,
43A like number he designated for the ways of the netherworld:
44Six hundred he made dwell in heaven and netherworld.
45After he had given all the commands,
46And had divided the shares of the Anunna-gods of heaven and netherworld,
47The Anunna-gods made ready to speak,
